extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students or researchers of satire/comedy, and writers interested in The Onion's style
extracted.subtask_description: Producing/parodying news-style satire in the manner of The Onion: mimic the voice, structure, and conventions of real news outlets while using incongruity, repetition, and format-specific tropes for comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial voice modeled after the Associated Press
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onion's articles cover real and fictional current events, parodying the tone and format of traditional news organizations ... with an editorial voice modeled after that of the Associated Press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a straight, formal news-writing register (AP-like) to heighten contrast between formality and absurd content. Use conventional datelines, inverted-pyramid phrasing, neutral third-person reporting, and newsy ledes to make the parody land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present mundane events as newsworthy, surreal, or alarming
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication's humor often depends on presenting mundane, everyday events as newsworthy, surreal, or alarming, such as "Rotation Of Earth Plunges Entire North American Continent Into Darkness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframe trivial or familiar situations as crises or major news items; escalate stakes or apply hyperbolic language. Example tactic: treat an ordinary occurrence with the gravity and sourcing of a national story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody the tone and format of traditional news organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodying the tone and format of traditional news organizations with stories, editorials, and street interviews using a traditional news website layout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimic structural elements—headlines, subheads, bylines, photo captions, editorial columns, vox pops, and standard website article templates—to satirize journalistic forms as well as content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan / straight-faced reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The straight-faced manner in which The Onion reports non-existent events ... has resulted in third parties mistakenly citing The Onion stories as real news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an unamused, factual tone to increase verisimilitude. Anti-pattern: being so realistic that readers take the piece as factual—be mindful of potential for confusion or legal risks (examples in article show third-party mistakes and occasional lawsuits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statshot (illustrated statistical snapshot)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Statshot", an illustrated statistical snapshot which parodies "USA Today Snapshots".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a small, graphic summary of statistics presented deadpan; make the stats absurd or revealing in a single punchy image/graphic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infographics (bulleted jokes on a theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Infographics", with a bulleted lists of jokes on a theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize multiple short jokes under a unifying concept in infographic form; keep items concise and visually scannable so the humor comes from theme-driven accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion columns and mock editorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion columns, including mock editorials, point-counterpoints, and pieces from regular columnists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt op-ed rhetorical strategies (strong thesis, persuasive framing, counterpoint structure) but invert or exaggerate viewpoints for satirical effect. Use recurring columnist voices when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bizarre horoscopes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create short, surreal horoscopes that parody the fortunes-and-personality genre; rely on strange specificity and incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slideshows parodying content-aggregation with click-bait headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Slideshows that parody content aggregation sites like Huffington Post and Buzzfeed, usually accompanied by a "click-bait"-style headline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimic listicle/slide formats and exaggerated teaser headlines while subverting expected content; the headline should promise a sensational or emotionally manipulative payoff that the slides then undercut.

rubrics_metrics.name: News in Photos (photo + caption, no story)
rubrics_metrics.description: "News in Photos" that feature a photograph and caption with no accompanying story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let a single captioned image carry the joke; imply an unseen story through a deadpan caption that reframes the image absurdly.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Voices (mock vox populi survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: "American Voices" (formerly called "What Do You Think?"), a mock vox populi survey ... There are three respondents ... who appear to represent a diverse selection of demographics. Although their names and professions change each time they are used, the same six pictures have been reused weekly for over 20 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a small number of recurring, archetypal respondent images with interchangeable names/professions to lampoon public-opinion pieces; brevity and stereotyped answers aid the gag. Reuse of photos can become a running gag and build familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial cartoon (deadpan parody of conservative cartoons)
rubrics_metrics.description: An editorial cartoon drawn by "Kelly" ... a deadpan parody of conservative editorial cartoons, as well as editorial cartoons in general. Many of the cartoons feature the Statue of Liberty, usually shedding a single tear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the visual language and motifs of editorial cartoons (symbolism, single-image commentary) but invert or exaggerate positions for satire; recurring visual motifs (e.g., weeping Statue of Liberty) reinforce the parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of the Year (satirical award feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Person of the Year award. For example, in 1996 the Denorex Man was chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create mock honors that mirror legitimate institutional awards, using the formality of such selections to lampoon cultural figures or phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'No Way to Prevent This' recurring story after mass shootings
rubrics_metrics.description: "'No Way to Prevent This', Says Only Nation Where This Regularly Happens", a story republished with minor edits after major mass shootings in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition of an identically structured piece to perform sustained social commentary; republishing with small edits highlights the pattern being critiqued rather than producing a novel joke each time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onion News Network: parody of 24-hour cable news visual/style
rubrics_metrics.description: Onion News Network — a parody of "the visual style and breathless reporting of 24-hour cable news networks like CNN."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replicate video-news production conventions (urgent music, graphics, breathless anchors, breaking-news framing) and then subvert content; in video, production value should match the target format to sell the spoof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted-genre parody (clickbait, TED talks, Vox explainers, sports shows, cooking videos, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: ClickHole satirizes 'clickbait' websites; video series and features parody a wide range of specific media genres (TED Talks, listicles, ESPN, Dr. Oz, Vox explainer style, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When satirizing a specific genre, study and mirror its surface conventions (tone, pacing, visual cues, structural beats) and exaggerate those conventions or expose underlying absurdities. Genre-specific mimicry increases recognizability and comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurring formats, characters, and fictional entities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onion uses recurring fictional figures and constructs (e.g., Fictional Publisher Emeritus T. Herman Zweibel; recurring photos; recurring anchors such as Dwight Richmond) and running gags (e.g., 'Global Tetrahedron' as a fictional megacorp).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop internal continuity—recurring characters, fictional institutions, and repeated motifs—for deeper satire and audience in-jokes. Recurrence builds a satirical world readers can recognize and expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: verisimilitude vs. reader confusion / real-world consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally, the straight-faced manner in which The Onion reports non-existent events has resulted in third parties mistakenly citing The Onion stories as real news; notable incidents and legal/PR fallout are cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that high verisimilitude can cause misattribution or public confusion; consider context, clear labeling (when appropriate), and potential legal/ethical implications when pushing realism. Use disclaimers or platform cues where necessary to avoid harmful misunderstanding.
